title: Gametogenesis, Fertilization, Implantation, and Early Embryogenesis
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows human development from the germ cell to the end of the embryonic period. It explains how sperm and oocytes are made and why their meiotic schedules differ, how a sperm is remodeled and activated, how fertilization blocks polyspermy and restores diploidy, and how the blastocyst implants and rescues the corpus luteum with hCG. It then applies these events to ectopic pregnancy and placenta previa, and ends with the bilaminar and trilaminar discs and the timing of teratogen sensitivity. Board questions usually name an arrest point, a cell layer, a day, or a risk factor and ask you to reason to the mechanism or the consequence.
prerequisites: Phases of mitosis and meiosis, crossing over, and cyclin and CDK control of the cell cycle
Hormonal control of the ovarian and menstrual cycles, including the LH surge and the corpus luteum (RE-6, RE-7)
Histology of the seminiferous tubule, Sertoli and Leydig cells, and ovarian follicles (RE-2)
Gross anatomy of the uterine tube, uterus, cervix, and rectouterine pouch (RE-2, RE-4)

connections.how: The trophoblast layers that implant in week 1 and 2 go on to build the chorionic villi and the placenta.
The LH surge releases the first oocyte arrest, and hCG acting on the LH receptor keeps the corpus luteum alive in early pregnancy.
Nondisjunction during the long oocyte arrest explains the rise in trisomy with maternal age.
Errors at fertilization produce complete and partial hydatidiform moles, and abnormal implantation sites produce previa and accreta.

blocks.text: Both sexes use meiosis to halve the chromosome number and recombine alleles by crossing over, but the programs differ in when they start, whether they pause, and how they divide the cytoplasm.

Spermatogenesis begins at puberty in the seminiferous tubules. Type A spermatogonia on the basement membrane divide by mitosis to renew themselves and to produce type B spermatogonia, which become primary spermatocytes. These move past the Sertoli cell tight junctions (the blood-testis barrier) into the adluminal compartment, finish meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes, and finish meiosis II almost at once to form four spermatids. Incomplete cytokinesis leaves each clone joined by cytoplasmic bridges, so it matures in step. The sequence takes about 64 to 74 days and depends on FSH acting on Sertoli cells and on a high local testosterone made by Leydig cells under LH.

Oogenesis is front-loaded into fetal life. Oogonia multiply by mitosis to a peak of about 7 million by month 5 of gestation, then enter meiosis I and stop in the diplotene stage of prophase I. Each primary oocyte, wrapped in flat follicle cells, forms a primordial follicle. Atresia leaves about 1 to 2 million at birth and about 400,000 at puberty; only about 400 to 500 are ovulated, and none are made after birth.

The prophase I arrest is held by the follicle. Granulosa cells pass cGMP to the oocyte through gap junctions; cGMP inhibits the oocyte phosphodiesterase, so cAMP stays high and maturation promoting factor (cyclin B with CDK1) stays inactive. The LH surge closes these junctions and lowers cGMP, cAMP falls, and the oocyte finishes meiosis I in the hours before ovulation. The division is unequal: a large secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body. The secondary oocyte then stops at metaphase II, held by cytostatic factor (Mos and MAPK signaling, with Emi2 inhibiting the anaphase promoting complex), and finishes meiosis II only if a sperm fuses with it.

blocks.text: Unequal division keeps mitochondria, stored mRNAs, and nutrients in one cell to support the embryo until its own genome switches on. The long arrest has a cost: cohesin holding homologs together erodes over decades, so meiosis I nondisjunction and trisomy rise with maternal age. Continuous spermatogonial division instead raises de novo point mutations with paternal age (sporadic achondroplasia).

blocks.title: Meiosis I or meiosis II nondisjunction
blocks.text: A child with trisomy 21 carries two different maternal chromosome 21 homologs (distinguishable near the centromere). Homologs separate in meiosis I, so failure there sends both different homologs into the gamete; sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, so failure there gives two identical copies. Two different maternal homologs therefore mean a maternal meiosis I error, the most common origin of trisomy 21, because female meiosis I spans the decades-long arrest while male meiosis I lasts weeks.

sections.title: Spermiogenesis, capacitation, and the acrosome reaction

blocks.text: Spermiogenesis converts a round haploid spermatid into a streamlined spermatozoon with no further cell division. Each new structure comes from an existing organelle, so a defect in that organelle predicts a specific sperm defect. The process occurs while spermatids are embedded in Sertoli cells, which then release the mature cells into the lumen (spermiation).

blocks.title: Structures built during spermiogenesis
rows: Golgi vesicles that fuse into a cap over the nucleus
Lysosome-like store of hyaluronidase and acrosin for crossing the zona
Missing dynein arms (primary ciliary dyskinesia) give immotile sperm
Mitochondria gathered in a helical sheath
blocks.caption: Golgi makes the cap, the centriole makes the tail, and mitochondria power it.

blocks.text: Testicular sperm are not yet able to swim forward or fertilize. They gain progressive motility during transit through the epididymis, where glycoproteins and cholesterol from epididymal and seminal fluid also coat the membrane and stabilize it. That stabilization protects sperm from releasing the acrosome too early, but it means freshly ejaculated sperm cannot fertilize an oocyte.

Capacitation is the removal of this restraint in the female tract, mainly in the uterus and uterine tube, over several hours (about 7 hours in humans). Albumin in tubal fluid extracts cholesterol, raising membrane fluidity, and surface glycoproteins are stripped. Bicarbonate entry activates soluble adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP and protein kinase A rise and many proteins become tyrosine phosphorylated. Intracellular alkalinization opens the sperm-specific CatSper Ca2+ channel, and the Ca2+ rise produces hyperactivated motility, a vigorous asymmetric beat that drives the sperm through the cumulus.

The acrosome reaction occurs only in a capacitated sperm. It is classically triggered by binding to the zona pellucida (ZP3 in teaching texts), and progesterone from cumulus cells can also trigger it. Ca2+ influx fuses the outer acrosomal membrane with the plasma membrane at many points, releasing acrosin and other enzymes that digest a narrow path through the zona. The reaction also exposes Izumo1 on the equatorial segment, which binds Juno on the oocyte membrane and is required for gamete fusion. A sperm that reacts too early, before reaching the zona, loses its enzymes and cannot fertilize.

Sperm passes the corona radiata and binds the zona
Ca2+ influx triggers acrosomal exocytosis

blocks.caption: Capacitation happens in the female tract; the acrosome reaction happens at the zona pellucida.

sections.title: Fertilization, the block to polyspermy, and completion of meiosis II

blocks.text: Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube, its widest and longest segment, where the tubal fluid and the ovulated cumulus-oocyte complex meet ascending sperm. The secondary oocyte remains fertilizable for only about 12 to 24 hours after ovulation, whereas sperm survive in the female tract for a few days, so most conceptions follow intercourse in the days just before ovulation.

Fertilization proceeds in three barriers. Hyperactivated sperm push through the corona radiata, aided by surface hyaluronidase that loosens the cumulus matrix. Zona binding triggers the acrosome reaction, and acrosomal enzymes cut a path through the zona pellucida. Finally Izumo1 binds Juno, and the sperm plasma membrane fuses with the oocyte membrane, so the whole sperm head and tail enter the oocyte cytoplasm.

Fusion delivers sperm phospholipase C zeta into the oocyte. It generates IP3, which releases Ca2+ from the oocyte endoplasmic reticulum in repeated oscillations. This single Ca2+ signal activates the egg in three ways. First, cortical granules beneath the membrane undergo exocytosis (the cortical reaction). Their protease, ovastacin, cleaves ZP2 so the zona can no longer bind sperm (the zona reaction), and Juno is shed from the oocyte membrane, adding a membrane block. Second, Ca2+ activates CaMKII, which removes Emi2; the anaphase promoting complex then degrades cyclin B and securin, so the oocyte finishes meiosis II and extrudes the second polar body. Third, metabolism and protein synthesis are switched on for cleavage. Unlike the sea urchin, mammals do not rely on a fast electrical block; the cortical reaction is the main defense.

blocks.title: Egg activation by the sperm calcium signal
steps: Sperm and oocyte membranes fuse
Sperm PLC zeta makes IP3
IP3 releases Ca2+ from oocyte ER in oscillations
Cortical granules exocytose; ZP2 cleaved; zona stops binding sperm
CaMKII removes Emi2; APC degrades cyclin B

blocks.caption: One Ca2+ signal both blocks polyspermy and releases the metaphase II arrest.

blocks.text: The sperm nucleus swells as protamines are replaced by maternal histones, forming the male pronucleus beside the female pronucleus. Each replicates its DNA; then their envelopes break down and both chromosome sets align on the first cleavage spindle, organized in humans by the sperm-derived centriole. The pronuclei therefore do not fuse as nuclei. The results are restoration of the diploid number, determination of genetic sex by the X- or Y-bearing sperm, and the start of cleavage. Sperm mitochondria are destroyed after entry, which is why mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the mother.

blocks.title: Errors at fertilization and their karyotypes
rows: Triploidy; often a partial hydatidiform mole with a malformed fetus
Sperm fertilizes an oocyte lacking maternal chromosomes
Complete hydatidiform mole with no embryo
blocks.caption: An excess of paternal genome drives trophoblast overgrowth, linking fertilization errors to the molar diseases of RE-13-H.

blocks.predict: If an oocyte were injected with a drug that blocked the rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ just before sperm fusion, what two things would fail?
blocks.explain: Cortical granules would not release ovastacin, so the zona would keep binding sperm and polyspermy could occur. The anaphase promoting complex would stay inhibited, so meiosis II would remain stuck at metaphase II and no second polar body or female pronucleus would form.
blocks.check: The three effects of the Ca2+ signal and the egg activation flow.

sections.title: Zygote to blastocyst, implantation, and hCG

blocks.text: Cleavage is a series of rapid mitoses without growth, so the blastomeres shrink with each division. Tubal cilia and muscle move it toward the uterus inside the zona pellucida, which keeps it from sticking to the tubal wall. At about the 8-cell stage the blastomeres compact, sealing to one another through E-cadherin and tight junctions, and by about day 3 a solid morula of 16 or more cells has formed. Inner cells become the inner cell mass (embryoblast), and outer cells become trophoblast.

The morula enters the uterine cavity about day 3 to 4. Trophoblast cells pump Na+ inward with Na+/K+ ATPase, water follows, and a fluid cavity (blastocele) forms, turning the morula into a blastocyst. The inner cell mass sits at one pole (the embryonic pole) and will form the embryo; the trophoblast will form the fetal part of the placenta. About day 5 the blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida, which frees it to attach.

blocks.title: Week 1 timeline after fertilization
rows: Compaction; inner and outer cells separate
Blastocele forms; hatching from the zona
Endometrium, usually posterior or anterior wall of the body
Trophoblast attaches at the embryonic pole
Syncytiotrophoblast invades; hCG enters maternal blood
blocks.caption: Days count from fertilization, not from the last menstrual period.

blocks.text: Implantation needs a receptive endometrium. Progesterone from the corpus luteum makes the secretory endometrium thick, vascular, and full of glandular secretions, and receptivity is limited to a short window in the mid-secretory phase (about days 20 to 24 of a 28-day cycle). At the embryonic pole the trophoblast differentiates into two layers. The inner cytotrophoblast is mitotically active and supplies new cells. The outer syncytiotrophoblast forms by cell fusion, has many nuclei and no cell boundaries, does not divide, and erodes the epithelium and stroma with proteases. The conceptus is fully embedded by about day 10, and endometrial stromal cells around it swell with glycogen and lipid (the decidual reaction), forming decidua.

Without pregnancy the corpus luteum regresses about 14 days after ovulation, progesterone falls, and the functional endometrium is shed as menses. The syncytiotrophoblast prevents this by secreting human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). hCG shares its alpha subunit with LH, FSH, and TSH, and its beta subunit closely resembles that of LH, so it binds the LH receptor on luteal cells and keeps them secreting progesterone and estrogen. The corpus luteum of pregnancy is required until the placenta makes enough progesterone itself, at about 7 to 9 weeks of gestational age. Serum hCG becomes detectable about 8 to 10 days after fertilization, roughly doubles every 2 days in early pregnancy, peaks near 8 to 10 weeks of gestational age, and then falls. Pregnancy tests detect the beta subunit because it is the part unique to hCG.

blocks.caption: Loss of the corpus luteum before the luteal to placental shift ends the pregnancy.

blocks.predict: In a pregnancy at 5 weeks of gestational age, what would happen if the corpus luteum were removed? What about at 12 weeks?
blocks.explain: At 5 weeks the corpus luteum is still the main progesterone source, so progesterone would fall, the decidua would break down, and the pregnancy would be lost. By 12 weeks the syncytiotrophoblast makes enough progesterone itself.

sections.title: Abnormal implantation: tubal ectopic pregnancy and placenta previa

blocks.text: The blastocyst implants wherever it is when it hatches and becomes adhesive, about day 5 to 6. Normal implantation depends on two things: transport to the uterine cavity on time, and attachment to the upper uterine body. Delay produces an ectopic pregnancy; attachment too low in the uterus produces placenta previa.

An ectopic pregnancy implants outside the uterine cavity, and over 95% are tubal, most often in the ampulla. Anything that slows tubal transport raises the risk. The classic cause is prior salpingitis (pelvic inflammatory disease from Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae), which destroys ciliated cells and leaves intraluminal adhesions and partial obstruction. Other risk factors are a previous ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery including sterilization, pregnancy with an intrauterine device in place, assisted reproduction, and smoking, which impairs ciliary function.

blocks.title: From salpingitis to tubal rupture
steps: Salpingitis destroys cilia and scars the tubal lumen
Conceptus moves slowly and is still in the tube at day 6
Trophoblast invades the thin tubal wall without proper decidua
Tube distends; trophoblast erodes tubal vessels
Rupture, often about 6 to 8 weeks of gestational age
Hemoperitoneum pools in the rectouterine pouch
blocks.caption: Ampullary ectopics usually rupture in the first trimester; interstitial (cornual) ectopics, surrounded by myometrium, rupture later and bleed more.

blocks.text: The manifestations follow from this mechanism. The tube cannot support normal trophoblast growth, so serum hCG is lower than expected for dates and rises more slowly than the usual doubling. Because hCG still maintains the corpus luteum and progesterone, the endometrium undergoes decidual change, but curettings show decidua without chorionic villi, sometimes with the Arias-Stella reaction of enlarged, hyperchromatic glandular cells. The typical picture is amenorrhea, then lower abdominal pain and vaginal spotting as the stretched tube bleeds and decidua is shed. Rupture causes hemoperitoneum in the rectouterine pouch, the lowest part of the female peritoneal cavity in the upright position; blood under the diaphragm can cause shoulder pain referred through the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5); and large blood loss produces hypotension and tachycardia.

Placenta previa occurs when the blastocyst implants in the lower uterine segment, so the placenta covers the internal cervical os or lies close to it. Risk factors are those that damage or scar the upper endometrium or enlarge the placental area: prior cesarean delivery or uterine surgery, multiparity, advanced maternal age, multiple gestation, and smoking. In the third trimester the lower segment thins and lengthens and the cervix begins to efface, which shears the inelastic placenta from its base and opens maternal sinuses. The result is painless, bright red bleeding with a soft, nontender uterus. When previa lies over a cesarean scar, the decidua basalis is often deficient, so villi attach directly to myometrium (placenta accreta spectrum).

Premature separation of a normally sited placenta
Fetal vessels cross the membranes over the os
Maternal, often partly concealed behind placenta
Hemorrhage; accreta if over a scar
blocks.caption: Pain and the source of the blood separate the three.

sections.title: Bilaminar disc, gastrulation, and the period of teratogen sensitivity

blocks.text: In week 2 the implanted conceptus organizes into two layers. The inner cell mass splits into a dorsal layer of tall columnar epiblast cells and a ventral layer of small cuboidal hypoblast cells, forming the bilaminar disc. The amniotic cavity forms above the epiblast and the yolk sac below the hypoblast. Extraembryonic mesoderm lines the trophoblast, and the chorionic cavity opens within it, leaving the connecting stalk as the future umbilical cord. Syncytiotrophoblast lacunae tap maternal sinusoids about days 11 to 12, starting the uteroplacental circulation. Week 2 thus has two germ layers, two cavities, and two trophoblast layers.

Gastrulation in week 3 converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar disc and sets the body axes. The primitive streak appears about day 15 on the caudal epiblast, with the primitive node at its cranial end. Epiblast cells detach and migrate through the streak, driven by FGF8 signaling and the transcription factor brachyury. The first cells to pass displace the hypoblast and form definitive endoderm, the next spread between the layers as intraembryonic mesoderm, and the epiblast left behind becomes ectoderm. All three germ layers therefore come from epiblast. Nodal cells form the notochord, which induces the neural plate and later contributes the nucleus pulposus. Beating cilia at the node move fluid leftward and establish left-right asymmetry, which is why dynein defects can cause situs inversus. The streak normally regresses; a persistent remnant can give a sacrococcygeal teratoma.

steps: Primitive streak and node form on caudal epiblast
Epiblast cells detach and migrate through the streak
First cells replace hypoblast as definitive endoderm
Next cells spread between layers as mesoderm
Remaining epiblast becomes ectoderm
Nodal cells form the notochord, which induces the neural plate
blocks.caption: Epiblast cells displace the hypoblast; hypoblast does not become endoderm.

blocks.text: Sensitivity to a teratogen depends on the developmental stage at exposure. In weeks 1 and 2 the blastomeres and epiblast cells are still undifferentiated and can replace lost neighbors, so an injury either kills the conceptus or is repaired completely (the all-or-none period). From week 3 through week 8, each organ primordium is laid down in a narrow window of rapid proliferation, migration, and induction. Damage then removes cells or inductive signals that cannot be restored, causing major structural malformations. From week 9 (fetal period) organs mainly grow and mature, so exposures more often cause growth restriction or functional deficits, though the brain remains vulnerable.

blocks.title: Stage at exposure and typical outcome
rows: All or none: loss or normal development
blocks.caption: Gestational age runs about 2 weeks ahead of age from fertilization.

blocks.title: Dating an exposure
blocks.text: A woman with regular 28-day cycles is exposed to a teratogen on day 24 after her last menstrual period (LMP). Fertilization occurs about day 14, so exposure fell about 10 days after fertilization, in week 2, before gastrulation. The expected outcome is all or none: early loss or normal development. The same exposure on day 42 after the LMP falls about 4 weeks after fertilization, when the neural tube, heart, and limb buds are forming, so structural defects become likely, often before the pregnancy is recognized.

blocks.predict: Why does a toxic insult on day 10 after fertilization rarely cause a cleft lip or a limb defect, while the same insult on day 30 can?
blocks.explain: On day 10 no organ primordia exist and surviving cells can replace lost ones, so the embryo dies or recovers. By day 30 the face and limb buds are forming in fixed windows, and lost cells or signals cannot be replaced.
blocks.check: The teratogen paragraph and the stage table.

integration.text: The chapter rests on cell biology. The same cyclin B and CDK1 machinery that drives mitosis is held in check at two points in the oocyte, by cAMP in prophase I and by cytostatic factor in metaphase II, and a single Ca2+ wave at fertilization both releases the second arrest and blocks polyspermy. Errors at these checkpoints link directly to genetics and pathology: nondisjunction during the long prophase arrest produces maternal age-related trisomy, and failure of the polyspermy block or loss of the maternal genome produces triploidy and molar pregnancy. Organelles explain sperm defects, from the Golgi-derived acrosome to the centriole-derived axoneme whose dynein defects cause both infertility and situs inversus.

Endocrinology and microbiology meet at implantation. Progesterone from the corpus luteum prepares the endometrium, and hCG, acting through the LH receptor, keeps that support in place until the placenta takes over, which is also why hCG levels reflect trophoblast health in both normal and ectopic pregnancy. Sexually transmitted Chlamydia and gonococci damage tubal cilia and convert a timing problem into a tubal ectopic pregnancy, while surgical scarring of the uterus shifts implantation toward previa and accreta. Finally, gastrulation sets the timing of teratogen sensitivity; that timing, not the agent alone, decides whether exposure leads to loss, normal development, or a malformation.

summary: Spermatogenesis is continuous from puberty and gives four sperm per meiosis; oogenesis starts before birth and gives one ovum plus polar bodies.
Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I until the LH surge; secondary oocytes arrest in metaphase II until sperm fusion.
The long oocyte arrest favors meiosis I nondisjunction with maternal age; paternal age raises de novo point mutations.
Spermiogenesis builds the acrosome from the Golgi and the flagellum from a centriole and sheds cytoplasm as a residual body.
Capacitation in the female tract removes cholesterol and glycoproteins; the acrosome reaction occurs only after zona binding.
Fertilization in the ampulla triggers a Ca2+ wave that drives the cortical reaction (block to polyspermy) and completes meiosis II.
The blastocyst implants about day 6; syncytiotrophoblast hCG acts on LH receptors to keep the corpus luteum making progesterone.
Slow tubal transport after salpingitis causes tubal ectopic pregnancy, usually ampullary, with low hCG and risk of rupture.
Placenta previa lies over the internal os and bleeds painlessly in the third trimester as the lower segment stretches.
All three germ layers come from epiblast in week 3; weeks 3 to 8 are the period of greatest sensitivity to structural teratogens.

verify: Duration of human spermatogenesis is quoted as about 64 days (Langman and many review books) or about 74 days (Guyton and Hall); confirm which figure NABNE expects.

Oocyte numbers (about 7 million at month 5, 1 to 2 million at birth, about 400,000 at puberty, 400 to 500 ovulated) vary between texts and are stated as approximate; Langman gives about 40,000 at puberty.

The zona glycoprotein that binds human sperm and triggers the acrosome reaction is taught as ZP3 in older texts, while current work assigns sperm binding in humans largely to ZP2 with ZP3 and ZP4 contributing; confirm which NABNE expects.
The window of implantation (about days 20 to 24 of a 28-day cycle) and the timing of hCG detection in serum (about 8 to 10 days after fertilization) vary slightly between sources.
The timing of the luteal to placental shift is given as about 7 to 9 weeks of gestational age here; some sources say 8 to 10 weeks.
The percentage of ectopic pregnancies that are tubal (over 95%) and ampullary (about 70% to 80%) follows common review figures; confirm current values.
Current obstetric terminology classifies previa as previa versus low-lying placenta rather than complete, partial, and marginal; confirm which terminology NABNE uses.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects molecular names such as PLC zeta, Izumo1 and Juno, ovastacin, Emi2, and CatSper, or only the processes they mediate.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: meiosis-gametes (spermatogenesis and oogenesis side by side with arrest points), and bilaminar-trilaminar (week 2 and week 3 disc cross sections with cavities and germ layers).
